I want a real slot intersector on java.time that computes in instants and only converts at the edges. Participant.java — public record Participant(String name, ZoneId zone, TimeRange workday, List<TimeRange> busy). Fail-fast IAE per component: "name must not be null", "zone must not be null", "workday must not be null", "busy must not be null", and "busy must not contain null" for a null element. Store busy as an unmodifiable defensive copy. Busy blocks may arrive unsorted and overlapping — that's normalized later, not rejected.

Slot.java — public record Slot(ZonedDateTime start, ZonedDateTime end) with the same null checks ("start/end must not be null") and a Duration length() = Duration.between(start, end).

MeetingSlots.java — public final class MeetingSlots, one static entry point:
  public static List<Slot> find(List<Participant> people, LocalDate date, Duration minLength, ZoneId displayZone)
Validation, all IAE with exact messages: null or empty people → "people must not be empty"; a null element → "people must not contain null"; null date → "date must not be null"; null, zero or negative minLength → "minLength must be positive"; null displayZone → "displayZone must not be null".

- `date` is each participant's OWN calendar date. Their availability is workday.start to workday.end on that date in their zone, resolved with ZonedDateTime.of(date, time, zone) semantics: a time inside a spring-forward gap slides forward by the gap; an ambiguous fall-back time takes the EARLIER offset. Same resolution for busy blocks.
- Subtract each participant's busy blocks from their window (clamp to the window; merge overlaps; a block whose resolved span comes out empty or inverted — swallowed by the gap — is simply ignored).
- Intersect everyone's free intervals as instants; keep maximal common intervals whose real elapsed duration is >= minLength (inclusive); return them as Slots built with ZonedDateTime.ofInstant(instant, displayZone), ascending by start, in an unmodifiable list.
- Never use the system default zone or clock anywhere. All arithmetic in instants — the suite includes days where wall-clock math is off by an hour in both directions (US 2026-03-08 / 2026-11-01, Europe 2026-03-29 / 2026-10-25 boundaries) and windows that cross midnight UTC.

We're ripping out the cron library we vendored after last week's incident: it silently mis-handles day-of-month steps, and the only way to test anything built on it is to actually sleep until the schedule fires. I want our own scheduling core — deterministic, clock-injected, so CI can simulate a week of firings in microseconds. Module go-cronsched, package cronsched, this repo, stdlib only.

Layer 1 — expressions. Parse(expr string) (*Schedule, error) for classic 5-field cron: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, fields separated by any run of spaces/tabs, leading/trailing whitespace fine. Numeric only — reject JAN/MON style names. Each field takes *, single values, ranges a-b, steps */n and a-b/n, and comma lists mixing all of those (5,10-20/5,45). Bounds: minute 0-59, hour 0-23, dom 1-31, month 1-12, dow 0-7 where BOTH 0 and 7 mean Sunday. Everything else is an error that names the bad field: wrong field count, out-of-range values, reversed ranges (10-5), zero steps, a step on a bare value (5/2 — a step needs * or a range), empty list items, stray dashes, garbage.

On *Schedule:
- Matches(t time.Time) bool — minute resolution; seconds and nanos are ignored.
- Next(after time.Time) time.Time — the first matching minute STRICTLY after `after` (landing exactly on a matching minute returns the following one), seconds/nanos zeroed, computed as wall-clock in after's Location. If nothing matches within 5 years (think 0 0 30 2 *) return the zero Time — and don't discover that by crawling minute-by-minute across years; skip dead months and days whole.
- NextN(after time.Time, n int) []time.Time — the next n fires chained strictly forward; n <= 0 means an empty result, not a panic.
- The two day fields follow the classic cron either/or rule: a day field counts as restricted unless it is written exactly `*` (so */1 IS restricted even though it spans every day). When both dom and dow are restricted, the schedule fires when EITHER matches — 0 0 13 * 5 means Friday OR the 13th. Otherwise it's a plain AND.

Layer 2 — the part I actually care about. NewScheduler(now func() time.Time) *Scheduler; nil means time.Now, tests inject a fake. Entries are named: Add(name, expr string) error (parse failures propagate; empty or duplicate names are errors; a failed Add must not register anything), Remove(name string) bool. Sort by At, ties by Name. A clock that hasn't advanced (or jumped backwards — ntp happens) yields nothing, never re-delivers, never panics; cursors never move backwards.
